title: Tech & Software Questions
summary: 14 real behavioral questions tech candidates get asked, each with a STAR-style outline of the key points to hit.

sections.heading: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a technical decision made by your team or your manager.
sections.body:
Interviewers ask this to see whether you can hold a technical position under pressure without becoming difficult to work with — and whether you know when to let go once a decision is made. They're listening for how you disagreed, not just whether you were right.

Situation to set up: pick a real architectural or implementation choice — a database choice, a framework migration, a build-vs-buy call, a decision to skip test coverage to hit a date. Name the actual tradeoff, not just "I disagreed with my manager."

Action — hit these points:
- What you actually thought was wrong, in concrete technical terms (e.g. "the proposed schema would have required a full table lock on every write")
- How you raised it — a written doc, a design review, a 1:1 — and why you chose that channel over just objecting in the moment
- Evidence you brought, not just opinion: a prototype, benchmark numbers, or a postmortem from a similar past decision
- What happened when you were overruled, if you were: did you commit to the decision anyway, or keep relitigating it

Result to land: what actually happened to the system or the decision — did it get reversed, did your concern get addressed with a mitigation, or were you wrong and the original plan worked out fine? All three are fine answers if you're honest about it and show what you learned.

Watch out for: a story where you were simply right and everyone else was wrong. That reads as arrogance, not maturity. The strongest version of this answer includes a real concession — either you were partly wrong, or you disagreed and committed anyway.

sections.heading: Describe a time you had to learn a new technology, language, or tool quickly to get a project done.
sections.body:
This question is about your learning process, not the technology itself — hiring managers want to know if you can get productive in an unfamiliar stack without months of ramp-up, since most jobs require exactly that in the first quarter.

Situation to set up: use a real gap — you were a backend engineer suddenly needing to write React, a Python shop hired you but the on-call service was written in Go, or you'd never touched Kubernetes and inherited a cluster.

Action — hit these points:
- What your actual learning plan looked like in the first 48-72 hours (docs, a specific tutorial, reading the existing codebase, finding a teammate to pair with)
- A concrete first task you took on before you felt "ready," and why you didn't wait
- How you validated you were doing it right — code review comments you asked for specifically, a senior engineer you looped in, tests you leaned on because you didn't trust your own judgment yet
- Any scaffolding you built for yourself, like a personal cheat sheet or a small throwaway project to test assumptions before touching the real codebase

Result to land: a specific, measurable outcome — you shipped the feature in the timeframe that was asked, or you were doing production-level PRs within two weeks. Bonus points if you can say what you'd do differently now, since that shows the learning didn't stop at "I learned it."

Watch out for: vague answers like "I just read a lot of documentation and figured it out." Interviewers have heard that a hundred times. Name the actual resource, the actual first PR, the actual person you asked.

sections.heading: Tell me about a bug you shipped to production. What happened, and what did you do?
sections.body:
Every engineer has done this, so refusing to answer honestly ("I'm really careful, I don't really have one") is a bigger red flag than the bug itself. This question tests ownership and your incident hygiene, not your track record of never making mistakes.

Situation to set up: describe the bug precisely enough that a technical interviewer could picture it — a null check you missed, a migration that ran out of order, a feature flag that didn't get gated correctly and hit 100% of users, a race condition that only showed up under real load.

Action — hit these points:
- How you found out — did you catch it, did monitoring page you, did a customer report it, did a teammate spot it in the logs
- The order of operations: did you stop the bleeding first (rollback, flag flip, hotfix) before you fully understood root cause
- Who you communicated with and when — this matters more than people think; silence during an incident is its own failure
- The actual root cause once you found it, and the fix

Result to land: the blast radius, stated honestly — how many users, how much data, how much downtime, or that it was caught before it reached anyone. Then the follow-up: what changed afterward (a new test, a new alert, a change to the deploy process, a postmortem doc) so the same class of bug is harder to ship again.

Watch out for: a story that ends at "and then I fixed it." The strongest version of this answer is the systemic fix afterward — most interviewers care more about whether you changed the process than whether you're clever enough to have found the bug fast.

sections.heading: Describe a time you had to push back on a deadline or scope that felt unrealistic.
sections.body:
This is really a question about how you negotiate, not whether you're a pushover or a wall. Companies want engineers who protect quality and their team's health without being the person who says "that's impossible" reflexively.

Situation to set up: a specific ask — a PM wanted a feature shipped in one sprint that you knew needed two, or leadership wanted a launch date moved up ahead of a conference.

Action — hit these points:
- How you quantified the gap instead of just asserting it — a rough estimate broken into pieces, a list of what would have to be cut
- The alternative you proposed, not just the objection — a smaller v1, a phased rollout, extra headcount, or cutting a specific piece of scope
- Who you had that conversation with and how you framed the tradeoff in terms they cared about (risk to the launch, risk to other commitments, risk to reliability) rather than just "it's too much work"
- What you did if you were overruled anyway — did you flag the risk in writing, did you find a way to de-risk it (feature flag, extra monitoring, a smaller blast radius)

Result to land: what actually shipped, on what date, and whether your read on the risk turned out to be right. If it slipped anyway, that's fine — say what the fallout was and that you'd called it.

Watch out for: sounding like you just refused to do hard things. The best version of this story shows you did the math, offered a real alternative, and stayed constructive even under pressure to just say yes.

sections.heading: Tell me about a time you had to give a teammate hard feedback on their code or their work.
sections.body:
Interviewers are checking whether you can be direct without being harsh, and whether you default to silence when something isn't working — silence is usually the more common failure mode among engineers, so a real story here stands out.

Situation to set up: something concrete — a teammate's PRs were consistently missing test coverage, a junior engineer's code worked but was unreadable and slowing the whole team down in review, a peer kept merging without waiting for review.

Action — hit these points:
- Whether you gave the feedback in the PR itself or pulled the person aside — and why that channel, not the other one (public code review comments can feel like public shaming for the wrong kind of feedback)
- The actual language you used — specific and behavior-focused ("these last three PRs didn't have tests for the new branch, can we make that a habit") rather than vague ("your code quality needs work")
- How you made it a two-way conversation instead of a lecture — did you ask what was getting in their way (deadline pressure, not knowing the testing patterns, unclear expectations)
- Any follow-through — did you pair with them, point them at examples, check back in a week

Result to land: what changed, specifically — their next few PRs met the bar, or the conversation surfaced a real blocker (they didn't know the test setup existed) that was easy to fix once named.

Watch out for: a story where the "feedback" was really just a complaint you made to someone else, or where the resolution is vague ("and after that things got better"). Be specific about what you actually said.

sections.heading: Tell me about a project that didn't ship, or that failed. What did you learn?
sections.body:
This question filters for self-awareness. Everyone has a failure; the people who struggle here are the ones who either can't name a real one or who tell a failure story where they did nothing wrong and blame everyone else.

Situation to set up: a project that was genuinely cancelled, missed its goal, or shipped and had to be rolled back — not a near-miss you're dressing up as a disaster.

Action — hit these points:
- What you were responsible for specifically, so the interviewer can locate your role in the failure, not just the team's
- The decision point where things went wrong, in hindsight — under-scoping the problem, not validating an assumption early enough, optimizing for the wrong metric, not looping in a stakeholder soon enough
- What you did once it became clear it was failing — did you raise the alarm, try to salvage a smaller version, or let it run to the end
- The actual, specific lesson — not "communication is important" but something like "I now write a one-page spec and get sign-off from the consuming team before I start building integrations, because that project failed when the API contract changed under me halfway through"

Result to land: what you changed about how you work afterward, and ideally a moment later in your career where that lesson visibly paid off.

Watch out for: a humble-brag disguised as a failure ("my only failure is that I care too much and worked too many late nights"). Interviewers can tell, and it burns trust for the rest of the interview.

sections.heading: Tell me about a time you had to work with a difficult teammate or an underperforming team member.
sections.body:
This is a proxy for how you'll handle the inevitable friction of team work without escalating everything to a manager or quietly disengaging. Interviewers are listening for whether you tried to solve it at your level before going over someone's head.

Situation to set up: something specific and fair to the other person — a teammate who missed most standups, someone whose PRs took days to turn around and blocked your work, a peer who dismissed ideas in planning meetings.

Action — hit these points:
- What you tried directly first — a private conversation, adjusting how you worked around their pace, asking if something outside work was going on
- How you protected your own deliverables in the meantime without just working around the person permanently, which usually just hides the problem
- The point, if any, where you looped in a lead or manager, and how you framed it — behavior and impact, not character judgments
- What you learned about working styles that you'd apply differently next time

Result to land: how it actually resolved — the person improved, they moved to a role that fit better, or it stayed imperfect but you found a workable way to collaborate. Real endings, not fairy-tale ones, land better.

Watch out for: trash-talking a specific real person in a way that reads as unprofessional, and stories where the entire cause of the friction was the other person with zero acknowledgment of your part in the dynamic.

sections.heading: How do you handle competing priorities when everything on your plate feels urgent?
sections.body:
This is less about a single story and more about your operating system for triage — but the strongest answers still ground it in one real week rather than staying abstract.

Situation to set up: a real stretch — on-call rotation plus a feature deadline plus a teammate out sick, or three stakeholders each treating their request as the top priority.

Action — hit these points:
- The actual framework you used to rank things — impact and reversibility, who's blocked by what, what has a hard external deadline versus a soft internal one
- How you made priority visible to other people instead of silently deciding on your own — updating a ticket board, a quick message to a stakeholder saying "this will now land Thursday, not Tuesday, because X came in as P0"
- What you explicitly said no to or deferred, and how you communicated that
- Any tooling or habit you use day to day (a written priority list at standup, timeboxing, a personal rule like "anything that pages me at 2am gets handled before anything else")

Result to land: the outcome of that specific week — what got done, what got pushed, and that nothing silently dropped without anyone knowing.

Watch out for: answering only in the abstract ("I use the Eisenhower matrix") with no real example. Naming an actual framework is fine as a headline, but it needs a real week attached to it.

sections.heading: Tell me about a time you had to explain a complex technical concept to a non-technical stakeholder.
sections.body:
This tests whether you can translate, not whether you can simplify to the point of being useless. Interviewers want engineers who make their non-technical partners smarter, not ones who talk down to them or bury them in jargon.

Situation to set up: something with real stakes — explaining to a sales lead why a feature they promised a customer would take three sprints, telling a CEO why a security fix required downtime, walking a support team through why a bug they were escalating as "the whole system is down" was actually a caching issue affecting a small percentage of users.

Action — hit these points:
- The actual analogy or framing you used, and why you chose it for that audience specifically
- What you deliberately left out because it wasn't relevant to their decision, versus what you kept because it changed what they'd choose to do
- How you checked they actually understood — did you ask them to repeat it back, did you follow up in writing so there was a record
- Whether the conversation changed a decision they were about to make, which is the real test of whether the explanation worked

Result to land: the concrete decision or outcome that followed — they adjusted the customer commitment, they approved the downtime window, the escalation got correctly reprioritized.

Watch out for: a story that's really about how smart you sounded rather than what the other person walked away understanding and deciding. The measure of success here is their decision, not your explanation.

sections.heading: Describe a time you took on work outside your job description or your comfort zone.
sections.body:
Growing companies need engineers who will pick up a gap even when it's not technically "their job" — this question is checking for that instinct versus a rigid sense of lane-staying.

Situation to set up: something real and slightly uncomfortable — a backend engineer who ended up doing customer interviews because no PM was staffed on the project, a junior engineer who ran a postmortem because the senior engineer who usually did it was out, picking up basic infrastructure work because the team had no dedicated infra person.

Action — hit these points:
- Why you stepped in specifically — was it obvious no one else would, did someone ask you directly, did you see it blocking something you cared about
- What made it uncomfortable, named honestly (you'd never run a meeting like that before, you didn't know the tooling, you were worried about overstepping a role that wasn't yours)
- How you got up to speed fast enough to actually be useful rather than just present
- Who you leaned on for help, since doing this entirely solo and silently is usually less impressive than knowing when to ask

Result to land: the concrete outcome, plus whether it changed your role going forward — did you keep doing that kind of work afterward, did it lead to a title change or new responsibility.

Watch out for: answers that are really just "I worked really hard" with no actual unfamiliar skill or discomfort in them. The point of this question is stretch, not extra hours.

sections.heading: Tell me about a time you disagreed with feedback on a pull request or code review.
sections.body:
This is a narrower, more concrete cousin of the general disagreement question, and interviewers ask it separately because code review is where a huge amount of day-to-day friction actually lives.

Situation to set up: a specific review comment — a reviewer wanted you to abstract something you thought was premature, wanted a pattern you thought didn't fit the codebase, or blocked a PR over a style preference you didn't think was worth the delay.

Action — hit these points:
- What the actual disagreement was about, technically, so it's clear you understood their point and it wasn't just stubbornness
- Whether you responded in the PR thread, took it to a quick call, or looped in a third person to break the tie — and why
- Any compromise you proposed rather than a flat no (ship it now and file a follow-up ticket, do it their way but leave a comment explaining the tradeoff for next time)
- How you kept the tone collaborative in a medium that strips out tone easily and turns disagreements sharp fast

Result to land: what actually got merged, and whether time proved either of you more right — a good ending here is often "we were both partly right and the eventual approach was better than either original version."

Watch out for: turning this into a story about a reviewer who was simply wrong or difficult. Even if that's true, the interviewer is testing your conduct in the exchange, not refereeing who was correct.

sections.heading: Walk me through how you have handled being on-call or responding to a production incident.
sections.body:
This question separates people who've actually carried a pager from people who've only read about incident response. Specificity about the mechanics — paging tools, severity levels, who gets looped in — is what makes an answer credible.

Situation to set up: a real page — an error rate spike, a downstream dependency outage, a deploy that broke something in a way tests didn't catch, a database running out of connections under load.

Action — hit these points:
- How you triaged severity in the first five minutes — customer impact, whether it was still getting worse, whether it needed to be escalated beyond you
- The mitigation-before-root-cause sequence — rollback, feature flag off, scaling up a service, failing over — before you fully understood why it happened
- Who you communicated with and how often (a status channel, an incident commander, a stakeholder update cadence) even before you had the full answer
- What the postmortem covered afterward, and specifically whether it was blameless — focused on the process and system gaps, not on who to blame

Result to land: time to mitigate versus time to full resolution, stated as real numbers if you have them, plus the concrete follow-up items that came out of the postmortem and whether they actually got done. A lot of postmortem action items die unfinished — finishing them is a signal worth mentioning.

Watch out for: a story that stops at "we fixed it" with no postmortem, no communication plan, and no prevention. Mature incident response is as much about the after as the during.

sections.heading: Tell me about a time you had to make a technical decision with incomplete information.
sections.body:
Every real engineering decision is made with incomplete information — this question checks whether you can move forward anyway with a defensible process, rather than either freezing or guessing recklessly.

Situation to set up: something concrete — choosing an architecture before load patterns were known, picking a vendor or library without a full trial period, estimating a project's timeline before all the requirements were locked.

Action — hit these points:
- What information you genuinely didn't have, and why waiting for it wasn't realistic (a deadline, a cost to delay, a decision that unblocked other people)
- What you did to reduce the uncertainty cheaply before deciding — a quick prototype, a conversation with someone who'd done something similar, a time-boxed spike
- The actual decision rule you used once you'd done what you could — reversibility (can this be changed later cheaply), which mistake is cheaper to make, or picking the option with the best worst-case
- Whether you built in a way to catch it early if you were wrong — a metric to watch, a checkpoint date, a flag to roll back

Result to land: what happened once more information came in — did the decision hold up, and if it didn't, how quickly you caught it and what it cost to correct.

Watch out for: pretending you actually had enough information all along, which undercuts the whole point of the question. The honest, well-reasoned account of how you bet under uncertainty is far stronger than a story that quietly erases the uncertainty.

sections.heading: How do you think about technical debt versus shipping new features?
sections.body:
This is an opinion question, but interviewers are grading the reasoning, not the position. A good answer treats tech debt as a real tradeoff with costs on both sides, not a moral crusade in either direction.

Situation to set up: ground your framework in one real decision — a piece of legacy code you chose to leave alone because the risk of touching it outweighed the ugliness, or a spot where you did stop feature work to pay down debt because it was actively slowing the team down.

Action — hit these points:
- How you distinguish debt that's costing the team real velocity or reliability from debt that's just aesthetically unpleasing but harmless
- A concrete way you've made the cost of debt visible to non-engineers — time added to every feature touching that area, incident frequency, onboarding time for new hires
- How you've negotiated space to address it — a fixed percentage of each sprint, a dedicated week, bundling a cleanup into a feature that already touches that code
- An example where you deliberately chose to take on debt knowingly, and how you flagged it so it didn't get forgotten (a ticket, a TODO with context, a note in the design doc)

Result to land: a specific before/after — deploy time dropped, a class of bugs stopped recurring, onboarding a new engineer to that part of the codebase got faster.

Watch out for: a purist answer either way ("debt should always be paid down immediately" or "shipping is all that matters"). Both signal you haven't actually had to defend a prioritization call to a skeptical PM.
